utterances.text: Yes. Because it has been transcribed as the "19th of April." So there apparently was one of the very few mistakes in the transcript. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Were you aware that Sredoje Lukic was being held prisoner at a hydro-electric dam in Visegrad and was released immediately upon arrival of the Uzice Corps on April 15, 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that. I've never heard it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 6267, page 1 of the B/C/S original and page 2 of the English translation. The Prosecution requests this document not be broadcast to the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This document is an Uzice DB 3rd Administration report dated 4 June 1992 that relates to Sredoje Lukic and Niko Vucic who committed crimes in Visegrad. Directing your attention to paragraph which is -- the second paragraph from the bottom in your copy, it begins: "Upon the release from captivity in the Visegrad HE, they left their jobs as policemen. They stole a sour cherry-coloured Golf car with Sarajevo registration plates and left for Serbia. About a month ago, they returned to Visegrad." Based on the date of this report which is 4 June 1992, is it correct that the Serbian DB was aware Sredoje Lukic was not in Visegrad and returned in early May 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document would indicate that they knew that they had operative information, given the date of the document. But it says here that he first left Visegrad and then he returned to Visegrad. This is a statement based on the conversation with a source that took place in June, so he -- the document talks about something that is in the past.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This information also indicates that the Serbian MUP allowed Sredoje Lukic to leave and return from the Republic of Serbia; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The MUP of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, it doesn't say anywhere that the MUP allowed it. This is an interview which took place on the 30th of June, and the operative who conducted the interview learns what had happened. He learns that from the interview with the source. He learned of what had happened a month before the interview. This is just operative information that hasn't been checked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we -- before we -- Witness, you said this is an interview of the 30th of June. I see in my copy and in the original that it's the 3rd of June, not the 30th of June.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 3rd of June. I misspoke. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, please listen to my question specifically, and I'm asking you this in the context that this is the information that was available to the Serbian DB. That is well understood. The paragraph continues to state: "They set up their own group consisting of 30 individuals from Visegrad, Uzice, Belgrade and Smederevo. They presented themselves as White Eagles. They are accommodated in the Visegradska Banja spa in a bungalow in the immediately vicinity of the Vojina Vlas hotel. During that time they had liquidated by slaughter between 270 and 300 individuals of Muslim nationality." This paragraph references a particular incident and concluded: "They bring Muslim women to Visegradska Banja, rape them and then liquidate them by slaughter." The next paragraph states: "Such conduct on Vucic and Lukic's part," referring to Sredoje Lukic, "irritates loyal Muslims who have stayed on living in the area of Visegrad municipality that they too take up arms and fight against Serbs?" Sir, is it correct that the Serbian MUP possessed jurisdiction over crimes being committed by citizens of the Republic of Serbia who lived in Uzice, Belgrade and Smederevo?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether the court had jurisdiction to prosecute people who lived in Uzice and Smederevo? Is that what you're asking?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You had authority over citizens who resided in Uzice, Belgrade, and Smederevo; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, I think -- could I just object to the question. It's unclear. Authority to do what? Jurisdiction to do what? I think my learned friend should be specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Weber, I'm seeking the parties to agree on the following. Usually if a court has jurisdiction in relation to certain criminal behaviour, that entails also the competence of the investigative authorities of that state to investigate. I'm not saying where they would investigate but at least to -- because you can't prepare a case file for a case over which the courts have jurisdiction if the investigative authorities would have no competence to investigate. Do we agree on that? As a general rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes? Mr. Petrovic, you as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's good. Then in your question, Mr. Weber, I think it should be -- it should be perfectly clear that there is a distinction between the -- if I could call it the active personality principle, that is, that the jurisdiction of a state to investigate, prosecute and adjudicate crimes for their own nationals is not exactly the same as the jurisdiction to investigate, prosecute and adjudicate crimes by those who are -- have their domicile on -- in the territory of that state. Your reference to people living somewhere was unclear in this respect. Therefore, I invite you to rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If I could come back to it. I do understand what Your Honour is saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We were talking about jurisdictional issues and if we want to deal with them, we should be precise in our language. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, are you aware that the Lukic group did continue to slaughter the Muslim population of Visegrad, including two incidents where groups of Muslim women, children, and elderly were burned alive? Do you know of those incidents?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about them later. In fact, I mostly read about it in the press, found out about it from the media. It was not part of my work at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The information in this report directing you to -- if we could actually have page 2 of the B/C/S for the witness. It is at the bottom of page -- the page 2 in the English before the Chamber. This report includes information that: "Vucic and Lukic's group conducts looting in the area of the municipality of Visegrad. They transport the goods to Serbia by vehicle. At the check-points they use friendships which have been struck up earlier with their colleagues from the Uzice SUP as well as hand out bribes so that they take the goods into Serbia and sell it. I have learned unofficially that one of the heads of the Uzice SUP is helping them in these dealings." My question to you, sir, is: The Serbian MUP had the ability, the authority, to stop individuals at the borders that were transporting goods into Serbia that were proceeds of crimes; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It had the ability, it had the right to stop anyone trying to cross the border, if they had reason to believe the goods were stolen or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The information in this report indicates that Sredoje Lukic and Niko Vucic were not stopped by the Serbian MUP; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the document seems to indicate that. But it doesn't say what or when. It says they were crossing the border. It refers to prior friendships. I'm seeing this document for the first time, and it's precisely the state security sector as the creator of this report notes, that the SUP, the Secretariat for Internal Affairs, is not stopping them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time the Prosecution would tender 6267 into evidence under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objection. Mr. Registrar, the number would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number would be P3020, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P3020 is admitted into evidence, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At the end of October 1992, you received orders from Mr. Jakov Sokic to go to the Uzice SUP and conduct an interview of someone who was in custody; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that Mr. Sokic did not tell you over the phone who was this custody at that time?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly sit closer to the microphones. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you come a bit closer to the microphone, Mr. Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You've referred to the fact that you received a direct order from Belgrade to conduct this interview. How were you informed of that order?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was informed by Jakov Sokic. I came to the centre at his invitation, and he told me there was an order to conduct an interview with Milan Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm a bit confused about that. If Mr. Sokic did not tell you the name of the person in custody, how did you learn that it was Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I came to the centre, may I explain this in some detail? I was in my apartment. The chief of the centre called me to come to the centre. I came there. The chief told me, Milan Lukic, who had been arrested in the area of Priboj, needed to be interviewed on the orders of the leadership in Belgrade because in the meantime he had talked to the headquarters of the service with the administration in charge. It's standard procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did this order to interview Milan Lukic come directly from Jovica Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the leadership of the service. I suppose Mr. Jovica Stanisic knew about it, or perhaps it was the chief of the 3rd Administration at the time which dealt with extremism. Maybe he is the one who conveyed the instruction to Sokic. I don't know about that. But the subordination is clear. The chief of the administration in charge contacts the centre that is concerned, and the chief of the centre concerned invites whatever operative officer he believes to be best for the job.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you report everything that Mr. Lukic - referring to Milan Lukic - told you during your interview to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entire interview was recorded, and the most interesting passages from that interview were written up in a document, and that document was submitted to the public security sector but also to the chief of the relevant administration in Belgrade. The audiotape is normally kept for a month, primarily in order to be able to draft the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Once you arrived at the SUP, you learned Milan Lukic was detained at the Uvat [phoen] border crossing when he and another individual named Dragutin Dragicevic attempted to enter Serbia with a large quantity of weapons; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, correct. Carrying a side-arm and forged documents. Forged IDs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At the border crossing, Milan Lukic presented himself as Negos Popovic and provided the false identification in this name; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw that, and I heard that from the colleagues from the SUP of Uzice who took him into custody. And they received that information from Priboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that the Priboj SUP recognised Milan Lukic at the check-point, despite the fact that he presented himself as someone else?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I was told.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have Exhibit P2448 shown to the witness. At this time we ask that the document nod be broadcast to the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While waiting for this document, I might just raise a matter I had for gotten at the beginning of this session. Mr. Jordash, could I have for one second your attention. During the last break I was informed that the exact date for the videolink? Was not yet communicated. I don't know whether that has been restored. But that was the message I received so I would say could you please pay specific attention to communication of videolink --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm surprised by that. But one of the issues --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would, most important for me is, that there's no malcommunication. Please try to confirm, seek confirmation that there's no malcommunication.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. The problem is the current witness we don't know if he is coming that's [Overlapping speakers] ... issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that. Then perhaps he has to wait or whatever. But, as I said yesterday, you can't organise a videolink if you do not have a date.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I apologise for the delay. I'm surprised by that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Please try to get that resolved. I'm sorry to interrupt, Mr. Weber. I should have done that at the beginning of the session. I apologise for that. Meanwhile the document is on everyone's screen. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, before you is the Official Note that you compiled dated 2 November 1992. Does this first page of the Official Note accurately reflect the items that were found in the possession of Milan Lukic on 26 October 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 2 of the B/C/S and English of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yesterday, the Stanisic Defence paraphrased a portion of this statement further down in the paragraph containing the direct quotes of Milan Lukic. I'm going to read the actual statements contained in this paragraph and then have I some further questions for you. Is it correct that Milan Lukic told you the following: "I came to Visegrad from Zurich on 10 April but I went to Obrenovac first. And from there, I went with my relatives who are all natives of Rujiste, Visegrad to undergo training in Ilok officially as the Obrenovac group. Fifteen men. At the time -- at the same time when my group was undergoing training, a group from Zvornik was also there. It also consisted of 15 men and was led by a man called Bude. The train was provided by men called Pupe and Zoran, Red Berets and Knindzas. When the training was completed, we went to Visegrad where we placed ourselves under the command of the Visegrad SUP, as part of the Visegrad TO." Is that what Milan Lukic told you?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Milan Lukic indicated to you that he left Visegrad after the 10th of April, 1992, with relatives and he subsequently returned to the municipality. Did you seek to confirm whether the Serbian DB possessed information that his cousin --

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That he came to Visegrad on the 10th. Not that he left Visegrad. He came to Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, my statement was they left Visegrad after the 10th of April, 1992, with relatives and subsequently returned to the municipality. Did you seek to confirm whether the Serbian DB possessed information that his cousin, Sredoje Lukic, also left Visegrad around the same time as indicated in the note that I showed you earlier?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, all my knowledge about Milan Lukic is derived from this interview and my conversation with a colleague who conducted the next interview. I reported all that I found out from that interview to the relevant administration in Belgrade. And among other things, this report is used for further work on the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, if you could just -- that's a no; correct? And if you could please respond to my question that you did not do anything to check it.

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not do anything. I sent a report to the relevant organisational unit in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please wait for the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yesterday at transcript 13983, you provided the following evidence about this passage. Question that was put to you: "Now half way down that page, Lukic claimed that he was trained by Pupe and Zoran, Red Berets, Knindzas in Ilok. Did he ever claim that he was trained by the Serbian DB in Ilok?" And your answer was: "Well, he said exactly what is written here. I was not familiar with the subject so I quoted him in that part." Are you saying that you had never heard of the Red Berets, Knindzas, before October 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whatever Milan Lukic said I quoted verbatim. I was no not in a position to comment on who Knindzas and Red Berets were. I heard about Knindzas, but who they were and what they were -- so I was not competent to comment on this piece of information. I just reported that passage of the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, please listen to my questions clearly. I'm asking you about your knowledge independent of the document. Are you saying that you had never heard of the Red Berets or Knindzas before October 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was reported in the media about Red Berets and Knindzas. I didn't know anything about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If you didn't know anything about this and you were interested in extremist activities, why then did you not ask Milan Lukic to clarify what he said to you concerning these units?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My priority in interviewing Milan Lukic, for which I was briefed by a man from the Territorial Defence who was familiar with that theatre of war, was to try to get information from him that would indicate he was involved in the kidnapping in Sjeverin. I put in the report item by item whatever he said. But at that moment when the interview was conducted, I was not qualified to talk to him about those units, and that's the main reason. First of all, I didn't want to show my ignorance about those units.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you seek to confirm, so I'm speaking about your actions subsequent to the interview, whether the Serbian DB possessed any information about any training facilities in Ilok or the Red Berets, Knindzas?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly not. That was not of interest to me. I was doing counter-intelligence work, and this is my only participation in this kind of interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you check whether the Serbian DB possessed any information related to either an individual named Pupe or Zoran?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 6200, page 9 of both the B/C/S original and the English translation shown to the witness. This exhibit contains the personnel file of Nikola Pupovac, aka Pupe, received from Republic of Serbia. The Prosecution requests that that exhibit not be broadcast to the public at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we know what the Prosecution intends to do with the document because the witness has said he doesn't have information. So if my learned friend is seeking to follow Your Honours' guidance concerning the tendering -- sorry, the use of documents during cross-examination then he ought to indicate what information he expects to elicit from a witness who says he doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it would be fairly obvious from the page I'm calling up. If not, I could further explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I know what the document says, or I know what the document purports to indicate, but that's not the issue. The issue is what my learned friend wants to do with it in light of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first hear what the witness's answer is. Because to speculate on what will happen later is not what I'm seeking to do at this moment. Mr. Weber, we have the document now in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If I could also please have page 9 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The document before you is from the personnel file of Nikola Pupovac, aka Pupe. This document is a request for admission into the active service --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I do beg your pardon but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you mean that Mr. Weber is already interpreting the document by ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: By claiming the nickname Pupe which hasn't been established through this document. It's a comment by Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it has been established through other evidence in this case. I had specifically referred to Exhibit P1001 correlating the nickname. If I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. And you take it for certain that that's evidence which is truthful and it could well be, I don't remember it exactly. But I think the appropriate way of dealing with the matter would have been that this is a file in which Mr. Pupovac, where other evidence has -- suggests that Pupe was the name also used by this person. If would you have introduced him in that way, I don't think that Mr. Jordash would have had any -- any objections. We're looking now at document which is in relation to Mr. Pupovac, and there's other evidence in this case in which it is suggested that Mr. Pupovac was also known by the name Pupe. Mr. Weber, what's your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This document is a request for admission into the active service of the Republic of Serbia MUP special purpose unit dated 21 April 1992. The request indicates it is from Nikola Pupovac who was stationed in Ilok. Now that you see there's corroboration of a Serbian MUP special purpose unit in Ilok in April 1992, does this impact your views on who trained Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you, I'm looking at this now. It just says the MUP of Serbia. It doesn't say State Security Service. I don't know this person.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yesterday at transcript page 12054 to -55, the Simatovic Defence showed you a JATD per diem payment list from the send half of November 1994. Nikola Pupovac is listed on 45 of these payment records of the JATD --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, may I stop you here for a second. This witness has, as he told us, made an Official Note of an interview he had with Mr. Lukic, in which Mr. Lukic told him that he was trained by a person by the name of Pupe. Okay. Now there is all kind of other evidence. What we would like to know is what this witness can tell us more about that. Not -- and that's what you are doing. You are asking this witness to combine that information with all kind of other information and then to draw conclusions that it must have been Mr. Pupovac. Whereas, this witness has no knowledge about that. Of course, it might well be that on the basis of the evidence of this witness and the other evidence that the Chamber would reach such conclusions or not reach such conclusions, also in view of whether there's any evidence which contradicts this, and then it's for -- but what is the use, if the witness doesn't know anything about it, to ask him to interpret the documents and the document he drafted. He has any personal knowledge about it, fine. Ask him about it. But do not say, Well, Mr. Lukic told you it was Pupe. Now, if you see this and this and this, would you agree with me that inevitable it must have been Mr. Pupovac? I mean, you're asking him to draw conclusions on the basis of a tiny little bit of the evidence he gave himself and all kind of other evidence on which I think it would be guided by the parties interpreting that evidence. It would finally be for the Chamber to establish whether Mr. Lukic was trained or not trained, if that is a relevant issue, by Mr. Pupovac. That is, I think, the procedural situation we find ourselves in. So if the witness could add anything more, and I think he said that he didn't have any knowledge beyond what Mr. Lukic us, but if he has any further knowledge, ask him about it but don't ask him to interpret the various pieces of evidence to see whether what he heard from Mr. Lukic should lead us to draw certain conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, of course, I will follow the Chamber's guidance. I was -- that is what I will do. At this time, the Prosecution tenders this exhibit into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Mr. Registrar, the number would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Next number would be P3021, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P3021 is admitted into evidence. Under seal, Mr. Weber or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm looking at the time. Is this a opportune time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's time for a break. We resume at a quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I'd like to raise a matter, and I think, Mr. Novakovic, to some extent, it might affect you as well. So it's -- it's -- it's the following: We are hearing the evidence of a witness who was scheduled for -- in my briefing it said two hours but it may have been two and a half hours. We're now three and a half -- a viva voce witness. We're now here three full days and it appears to me that we'll not finish the testimony of this witness. I have, here and there, been critical on the way in which the examination-in-chief and cross-examination was conducted. I verified, I always spoke on behalf of my colleagues as well. They fully share my views I expressed. We also had great problems with notice. That's for sure. It has been admitted. So I would say things did not go as they should have gone, and the Chamber is not satisfied that we could do it in a similar way in the future. Now we have scheduling problems for next week, to some extent the problems, Mr. Jordash, with the witnesses are beyond your control. Sometimes some earlier action might have led to easier solutions. Okay, but let's forget about that. For next week, as matters stand now, Tuesday, either there's a videolink. There, again, the malcommunication. I mean, the working can start only today where I already emphasised yesterday how important it was to have a date, because every day counts if you are preparing a videolink. Okay. For next Tuesday, we either have a videolink in which case, we are having difficulties because a videolink is difficult to -- to -- to delay, and then we would not have heard all the evidence of Mr. Novakovic. He would then have to wait, which is good for no one, or we have no videolink, in which case Mr. Novakovic has to wait for -- for quite a while for the last portion of his evidence. Therefore, the Chamber suggests that we would sit, although it would most likely be 15 bis tomorrow, but I would like to hear from the parties. Mr. Weber, where are we? And I already put a flag here. What I earlier said and I have not spoken out everything that was on my mind, the cross-examination was not always very effective, and was also not always direct and focussed. How much time would you still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution is endeavouring to do its best and I will try to conclude in -- in a full session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In this session we have another --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yeah. Your Honours, there were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- 55 minutes to go. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: There are some things we'd like to put on the record, though, with respect to the witness, though, which believe that we are still conducting further investigation and we did receive -- so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That is all that has to do with the notice and it has to do with possibly that you would like to recall the witness. Let's, at this moment, stay away from that. Mr. Petrovic, how much more time would you need with the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, between 15 and 20 minutes, not more than that. With your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: As matters stand, 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Which would mean that with a relative short session tomorrow, we might conclude the testimony of this witness. Of course, then the next question is about Mr. Stanisic's medical condition. I know that it is not welcomed to sit a fourth day. It would certainly not, on the basis of what I've heard until now, it would be a relatively short session. I also make the following comment that when we have been sitting for more than three days, it was not often and always after consultation with the parties. I also emphasise that for a very relatively short session, then, of course, the option of the videolink with the United Nations Detention Unit remains open. Therefore, I would like, having said all this, I would like to hear from the parties whether they would agree to have a relatively short session tomorrow, to finish hearing the evidence of Mr. Novakovic, and then, on Tuesday, we do not know, it might well be that this extra day will be compensated by not sitting on Tuesday anyhow, because the videolink is not technically already prepared, but it could also be that if the videolink is there, that we would then also sit on Tuesday where it is uncertain for how long next week we would sit, whether there would be any other day in which we would not be sitting. So it is a bit uncertain, everything, but the suggestion is that we finish at least the testimony of Mr. Novakovic tomorrow. Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I just add for Your Honours' information that our best estimate as to the length of the next witness, the videolink witness, would be -- that he would be completed in two days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Which leaves it open that perhaps next week the third day would -- depending on what happens with the witness on which we have still uncertainty, that is Witness DST-040, I think. So there are uncertainties. At the same time, a videolink is reserved, is prepared, and then someone is sent there, so to delay that is rather problematic. If it could, for example, be established for Wednesday, not on Thursday -- on Tuesday, then we might have an empty Tuesday and then finish that -- it's all uncertain. But our suggestion is that we would finish hearing the testimony of Mr. Novakovic tomorrow in a relatively short session. I can imagine that you perhaps want to consult with Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which you can do immediately, if you wish to, because it all requires some organisation as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Simatovic would like to be present via videolink tomorrow, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And has -- does this mean that he says, If I can be present through videolink, then I do not oppose this suggestion. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's how we understand it. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if this is your decision, we are fully prepared to sit tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It may have been clear -- if you have listened well to me, we have not decided any matter and we are seeking the input of the the parties. So if you say, Well, even if it's not your decision, we do not oppose such a decision then it is well understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We do not object, Your Honour. However, we have sensed a certain degree of preference in the tone of your voice, which is why we will go along with your decision, whatever it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Preference and decision is to be clearly distinguished. Mr. Weber, what's your preference.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: We're available whenever it is most convenient for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, you have followed our discussion. What we would like to do is to have a short session tomorrow and then excuse you after that so that you can travel home and you don't have to wait until the beginning of next week. I take it that that's no problem for you? Yes. Then, Mr. Weber, please proceed. And one -- one -- one last question. If we need a short session we could just start at 9.00. We also could consider to start a bit later. As long as we know for sure that we finish, we could, for example, start at 10.00 or 10.30. If that would accommodate Mr. Stanisic, even a bit more, then we would consider that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: 9.00 is fine. Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 9.00 is fine. Then it is hereby decided that we will have a session tomorrow morning at 9.00. And, as I said before, most likely we'll sit 15 bis. Mr. Weber, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, following your interview, Milan Lukic was released from custody a few days later; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. As far as I know, he continued being remanded in custody. He was taken over by the public security, once he was interviewed, and I believe that they were kept in custody, him and his colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it your testimony, then, that Milan Lukic was detained for more than 48 hours? Or do you not know?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that after the interview, after we took his statement, he was transferred to a detention unit. What happened then, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you were never called to testify at a hearing or trial related to the Sjeverin murders?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the trial that took place in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm asking you, Milan Lukic was detained in custody, and you've explained that you were investigating him for Sjeverin.

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 6269.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, coming up before you will be the Belgrade District Court judgement dated 15 July 2005 against Milan Lukic for the murders committed at Sjeverin on 22 October 1992. Could you please review the first paragraph of this judgement and confirm the fact that an indictment was not filed for these murders until 17 October 2002?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It is correct, then, that an indictment was not sought against Milan Lukic for the murders at Sjeverin until after Mr. Stanisic had left the office?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, that -- objection. That's quasi-logic, respectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it is about a point in time. Mr. Weber, there -- the appropriate way of dealing with the matter is to ask the witness whether he knows when Mr. Stanisic left office and then to say whether it is after or before. If we establish the date, if we have the two dates, the Chamber is still able to see which is the latter date and which is the earlier date. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When did Mr. Stanisic leave office?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say with any degree of certainty when Mr. Stanisic was pensioned off. I believe that that was in 2008, or perhaps 2009. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, whether that is accurate information can seriously be doubted. Do the -- have the parties --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1998, actually. 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have the parties any dispute about when Mr. Stanisic left office.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay and the date was? The year date?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 1998. Okay, fine. Then we have an indictment before us which, as the judgement says, was issued the 17th of October, 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry. My objection, Your Honour, was not that point precisely. My objection was that to go from looking at an indictment which is dated in 2010 and then to suggest to a witness that an indictments wasn't sought until then, that's the quasi-logic. We don't know at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. The only thing at this moment that we can establish is that this judgement refers to the date of 17th of October of 2002 as the date on which the indictment was issued. There we are. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If the Prosecution could please have the lower portion of the first page here for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to direct your attention to the person who is the third accused in this case. The co-accused in this case was Dragutin Dragicevic. Is this the same individual who was this custody with Milan Lukic when you interviewed him in 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the other person's name was Dragutin Dragicevic. I did not interview him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to Mr. Dragicevic after he was detained by the MUP in 1992? Do you know when he was released?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know absolutely, no. My only activity involving them was that interview. The rest was within the authority of the 3rd Administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time the Prosecution would tender 6269 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objection. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Next number would be P3022, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P3022 is admitted into evidence. No need to have it under seal, Mr. Weber?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, are you aware that less than a year after you interviewed him, Milan Lukic committed a second similar massacre of non-Serbs when he and his group took from a passenger train these individuals at Strpci. Are you aware of that incident?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you personally investigate that incident?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had nothing whatsoever to do with the investigation of that incident. The only involvement on my part concerning Milan Lukic was that interview that I conducted in -- in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to go back to a topic that we talked about earlier, and it was something that was somewhat confusing so I'd like to try to go through it with you in a clearer fashion. It relates to the question where funds came from that were used for payment of Serbian DB officials. Sir, I'm going to read a quote to you from your testimony yesterday at pages 14006 to 14007. You stated: "I've said I'm not an expert in financial matters, but I'm able to understand that much. At that time, by virtue of a decision made by the Republic of Serbia, a certain fund was established for payments to members of the special police unit who went on field missions in the territory of -- of the Republic of Serbia and every member of the State Security Service, that is, the special police unit, was paid from that fund whenever they went to other areas to assist." What do you know about this fund?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely nothing. I said that I saw that in the title of the document. The document showed that a decision was made by the Presidency of Serbia, and that, based on that decision, per diems were paid. I suppose that fund had been established within the Ministry of the Interior as part of budgetary resources or funds.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 1D5062.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, could you please look at the title of this document that you were referring to. Do you see any reference in this title to a fund?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The payment of per diems to special police units in keeping with the Presidency decision. That's how I'm reading it. Per diems were paid in keeping with the decision of the Serbian Presidency. I may have just decided to call it a fund, although it perhaps wasn't even a fund.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the answer to the question. No reference is made to a fund in this document. Only a reference is made to per diems paid in accordance with a decision. Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution this time please have 65 ter 4865; page 1 of the B/C/S, and page 2 of the English. Mr. Novakovic, I'd like to look at what Slobodan Milosevic has to say. This is a statement to an investigating judge in Belgrade on 2 April 2001 after his arrest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry. In our submission, the Prosecution ought to indicate again precisely what they intend to do. Because this looks very much like it's an attempt to put in this documentary rather than an attempt to actually elicit evidence from the witness. The witness has been clear that he -- if you wouldn't mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. Mr. Jordash may finish his line.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The witness has been cross-examined uphill and downhill concerning his knowledge abut financing. He has been very clear, in our submission, concerning what he doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's -- I -- one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied, Mr. Jordash. Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to direct your attention to a specific paragraph of this statement of Slobodan Milosevic. The paragraph states: "As regards the resources spent for weapons, ammunition and other needs of the Army of Republika Srpska and the Republic of Serbian Krajina, these expenditures constituted a state secret, and because of state interests could not be indicated in the Law on the Budget which is a public document. The same applies to the expenditures incurred by providing equipment from a needle to an anchor for the security forces and special anti-terrorist forces in particular from light weapons and equipment to helicopters and other weapons which still remain where they are today, and this was not made public because it was a state secret, as was everything else that was provided for the Army of Republika Srpska. In my opinion, these matters should still constitute a state secret, but court organs can certainly look into them. These anti-terrorist forces today still carry the heavy burden of security-related tasks in the south of Serbia." My question to you is: Is this the same fund that you were referring to with respect to the per diems?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I don't want to go behind Your Honours' order but the question has confirmed, in our submission, our suspicion which is that it's not designed to elicit evidence. It is designed to have this document tendered. Because the witness has made it very clear. He doesn't know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, no, Mr. Jordash. I -- Mr. -- your objection at this moment is denied. The document is not yet tendered. We will consider whether or not it will be admitted if Mr. Weber tenders it, but he is, at this moment, allowed to put this to the witness. Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, is this the same fund that you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, I keep telling you that I'm not a financial expert to be able to discuss to which fund it belongs. There is a paper that shows the names of myself and a colleague that speaks to the form of remuneration our employees received for certain missions, and it says that it was keeping with a decision of the Presidency of Serbia. I don't know whose and what intent it was, but it shows clearly that the funds were paid out from the budget of the administration that was put in charge of those things within the state security sector at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time the Prosecution tenders this exhibit into evidence. We're offering it though -- the witness writes as his credibility -- the witness was shown a document that didn't say anything about a fund and then supplied additional information outside the title of a document that discussed a fund. We are now offering information that shows that a fund existed and it went more -- just to add to that segment, it also didn't say anything about people being dispatched outside of Serbia, which the witness also added in his answer. We are now offering this as it relates to this evidence that was offered by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Only for credibility reasons or also for the truth of its content, Mr. Weber?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We accept that the document could be tendered for the impeachment purposes. What value it has is another issue, but we accept it could be put for impeachment purposes. For truth of its content, there is no basis being argued and no basis is before the Court and no basis is reasonably discernable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Simatovic [sic] any ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we are opposed to any kind of admission of this document. First of all, it was misrepresented. Mr. Weber refers to it as a statement of Slobodan Milosevic. It's not a statement of Slobodan Milosevic. It's a procedural document. It's an appeal by Slobodan Milosevic against a decision to remand in custody. What he wrote, why he wrote it, the context of the whole case, all these are uncertainties that cast large shadow on this document. This is it a procedural document. A decision to remand on -- into custody.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour, to both you and the interpreters. The gist is this: This is a document of procedural nature. It's not a statement, it's not an interrogation or a questioning. We do not know the circumstances under which Milosevic wrote this, if he wrote this. We do not know the circumstances of the case in question. I don't want to testify but I know that there was a large major case that may still be on trial in Belgrade. We don't have a statement before us. We have an appeal against a decision to remand in custody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will decide on admission of this document in due course. It will be marked for identification for the time being. Mr. Registrar, the number would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number would be P3023. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification under that number. Mr. Weber, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, of course the Prosecution is available should any further submissions be necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will consider whether on the basis of the submissions made until now whether it can reach a decision. If not, we will certainly invite you for further submissions. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yesterday at transcript page 13997, you stated with respect to a meeting on 8 November 1994 the following: "The meeting was chaired by Mr. Jovica Stanisic, and he told us that the meeting had been organised together with security and intelligence segments of the services of the Serbian Army of Krajina, the MUP, and the state security, and the aim of the meeting was to unify all the intelligence about the goings-on in the territory and stepping up the security level in the Krajina. The security was threatened by the refugees from the Autonomous Province of western Bosnia who arrived in the Republic of Serbian Krajina." My first question to you is: How do you recall the specific date of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How do I know about the nature of this meeting? I was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, it's about the date, the 8th of November. How do you remember that after 17 years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said the 8th or the 9th. I said clearly I'm not sure about the date, the 8th or the 9th of November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that the same question would apply, how do you know that it was exactly on the 8th or the 9th and not on the 7th or the 10th. And how do you remember after --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because I had arrived in Krajina two or three days earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Where did this meeting take place in Petrova Gora?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in a building right at Petrova Gora. There's some sort of facility there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: How did you arrive to the meeting?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two or three days earlier, I arrived in that region, and members of the service from the Republic of Serbian Krajina and myself came to that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you about a series of individuals who were present -- that you say were present at this meeting. If you could please just provide me with the names in response to my questions. Who was present from the SVK?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a man named Knezevic. I don't know his rank. And another one called Smiljanic [phoen]. I also don't know the rank. They were both from the security services of the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Who was present from the RSK DB?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this in private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in open session at this moment. Would you like to move into private session?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On transcript page 13993, you stated that before you left for Petrova Gora that you first went from Uzice to Belgrade and reported to the 2nd Administration. Who did you report to?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't now recall exactly who received us. One of the people from the administration met us there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you recall anyone that you met with during this occasion?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not meet anyone on that occasion. We were sitting in one office waiting, waiting to be taken somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'd like to refer to your -- some comments on your comments chart. Prior to your testimony here today, the Prosecution received your comments on two military reports from the SVK in August 1994. These exhibits are P1288 and P1299. You indicated the following with respect to these documents: You came to Pauk in November 1994; the documents show that information was just being provided to Jovica Stanisic so that he would be informed about what is going on; and Jovica Stanisic or the service did not have the capacity or the logistics to provide material assistance. Based on these comments and what you've said so far about Operation Pauk, is it your evidence that the role of the Serbian DB during Operation Pauk was limited to only information gathering?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can say about myself and the two colleagues from my service, members of the RDB of the Republic of Serbia, is that in the territory of Krajina, the northern part of Krajina, we were there only to collect counter-intelligence about the security situation in that territory, together with members of the service from the RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, your comments can be interpreted much more broad than what you are saying here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 6270 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, this is a Serbian DB JATD report from Janko Keris [phoen] dated 6 February 1995. As can you see from this report, at the very outset, it relates to the tasks performed by the JATD 1st Combat Group between 10 December 1994 and 1 February 1995. There are six tasks described in this report. Could you please read the first task entitled: "Command post security," and let us know when you need the next page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you turn the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I just asked to you read the first section, so we'll just go one by one. If you can let me know when you have completed the first section.

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, while you were in Petrova Gora, did you see command post security for the location that you went to?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I went there, I saw the place was secured by members of the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And you will agree with me that providing security for installations outside Serbia is something more than information gathering; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry. Objection. My learned friend is engaged, in our respectful submission, with the same kind of attempt to put documents into evidence using the guise of suggesting that it is eliciting evidence. The witness has, once again, said this is what me and my colleagues were doing. He hasn't said anything further than that. So to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, could you please rephrase your question --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe the witness has said something more than that at page 83, line 19, that he said that when I went there "I saw that the place was secured by members of the unit."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's apparently no the issue. You're asking the witness to tell whether an apple is the same as a pear. To the extent we have to decide that, we can do that ourselves. If you want to emphasise that what he saw -- let me check carefully. Yes. Mr. Novakovic, do you have an explanation for having seen persons providing security for installations where, as we took it from your answers, it was your understanding that the gathering of information was the main purpose of your people to be present at that spot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The reason my colleagues and I went into the field was to collect information. That meeting was indeed held at Petrova Gora, and there was security for the meeting, no question about that. However, about those activities that I see in the document, I know nothing. I'm seeing this for the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, I -- you may proceed, and for me, the matter is not concluded by the answer to my question, so if you want to further explore, you may do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, so you're clear as to the reason I'm asking about this document, it's because you offered many opinions about what was going on and the role of Jovica Stanisic during Operation Pauk. To further make this clear to you with respect to your comments on P1288, you stated that you think that: "Jovica Stanisic's presence at Operation Pauk occurred after the events relating of the fall of the APZB and I think that his role was to unify the data gathering of all the services with the aim of assisting the return of Fikret Avdic and refugees to improve the security?" Since you have expressed these opinions, I would like to deal with specifics as to what is reflected in the documents of the JATD. Could you please read the second section of this report entitled: "Convoy escorts." Have you read that second section?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 2, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Now your comments indicate that Jovica Stanisic or the service did not have the capacity to provide logistics. Do you consider the fact that the DB was actually providing convoy escorts as logistical support?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no clue what kind of convoy that was, what's the purpose of that convoy. My knowledge was certainly not at that level that I could know, because after that meeting, I was sent to the Slunj area and had no more -- anything to do with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. I want find out if you have knowledge about some of these other things and then I'll come back to your opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 2 of English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Directing your attention to section 3 of this report entitled: "Laying an ambush." Could you please read this short section and then let us know when you have completed the reading.

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you have any knowledge of joint operations being conducted with rocket-launchers or participation in combat operations by the members of the Serbian DB in Operation Pauk?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I had no knowledge about that. I was outside the unit, separate from the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. If could you please read the section entitled: "Reconnaissance."

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it your understanding that the information gathering performed by about the Serbian DB during Operation Pauk included daily reconnaissance of enemy positions, communications and facilities, in order to identify targets of operations? Sir, you don't need to read the document for that. Is that your understanding of what the information gathering was?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's also a kind of gathering of information, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is this the type of information gathering that you were taking part of [sic]?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 3 of both the B/C/S and English versions of this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so, Mr. Weber, I'm looking at the clock. I have a few messages to give to the parties, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could have then 15 minutes in tomorrow's session to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Fifteen minutes in tomorrow's session. Let's talk about tomorrow's session. I'm going to multiply every request by three, as would be perhaps the wisest thing to do. Tomorrow, Mr. Weber, you have not more than half an hour and that's strict, so I'll stop you at 30 minutes exactly. Mr. Petrovic, as matters stand now, you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, around 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That makes all together 50 minutes. You get not more than half an hour. Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thirty minutes, as matters stand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't get more than 40 minutes. I give already the bonus in advance --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- so as to avoid that -- which means that we have tomorrow a little bit over one session. And there may be questions by the Bench, we do not know yet, but we'll start tomorrow at 9.00. As far as next Tuesday is concerned, the preparation for the videolink seemed to proceed well. From the technical experts, we hear that they managed to have a videolink on the 11th and the 12th of October; that is, the Tuesday and the Wednesday. VWS seems to be well on its way to deal with everything they have to deal with, and there are another few other logistical matters which still have to be resolved. But there is a fair expectation that the videolink will work on Tuesday and Wednesday. Mr. Jordash you had scheduled this witness for examination-in-chief for two hours, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now two hours this week, meant, all together, three and a half days. I think that we should really give it now -- well, not for examination-in-chief but the total time for the witness was ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Two to three hours, I think we said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Well, apart from even if it would be three hours, the videolink most likely will function on Wednesday and -- on Tuesday and Wednesday. The Chamber expects from the parties to have a division of the time for those two days, calculating new questions that may arise, additional time you'd need because you're not present, whatever it is, and we'll be very strict on that. So that two hours examination-in-chief will certainly not be more than two days for the evidence of the witness in its entirety, and we'll be really more strict because the way it went this week was not acceptable. Mr. Novakovic, tomorrow we need you for a little bit over one session. We'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.00, and I, again, to the extent a human being can guarantee anything at all, but I can guarantee you that we'll conclude your testimony tomorrow morning, most likely in the second session. I again instruct you that you should not speak or communicate in any other way with anyone about the testimony, whether given during the three days you've testified now, or whether for the one and a half session tomorrow. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We stand adjourned, and we'll resume on Friday, the 7th of October, Courtroom II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 7th day of October, 2011, at 9.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
